course: Embedded Electronic Engineering A – Real-Time Systems

entries.objective:
Understand the Priority Exchange (PE) server algorithm for scheduling
aperiodic tasks alongside periodic tasks under Rate Monotonic scheduling
in real-time systems, including its mechanism, schedulability bound,
and trade-offs compared to other server algorithms (Polling Server,
Deferrable Server, Sporadic Server).
entries.prompt: In Real-Time system, explain "Priority Exchange" topic to me in detail
entries.ai_output_summary:
Explained Priority Exchange as a bandwidth-preserving server algorithm
for handling aperiodic tasks under Rate Monotonic scheduling. Key points
covered:

- Server defined by period Ts and capacity Cs; treated as periodic task
  with RM-assigned priority.
- Core mechanism: when no aperiodic request is pending, server exchanges
  its remaining capacity with the currently executing lower-priority
  periodic task — the periodic task runs at server's high priority, and
  the capacity migrates down to the periodic task's priority level.
- Capacity "trickles down" through priority levels until consumed by an
  aperiodic request or discarded at the lowest level.
- Schedulability bound formula provided (Liu & Layland-style, adapted
  for server utilization Us).
- Comparison table of PS, DS, PE, SS covering capacity preservation,
  response time, and complexity.
- PE has better schedulability bound than Deferrable Server (avoids
  back-to-back effect) but high implementation complexity.
- Historical note: Sporadic Server later offered comparable bounds with
  simpler implementation, so PE is mostly of theoretical importance.

entries.reflection:
Gained a clearer understanding of where Priority Exchange sits within
the family of server-based scheduling algorithms for aperiodic task
handling under Rate Monotonic scheduling. The key insight was the
distinction between bandwidth-preserving and non-preserving servers,
and specifically why PE achieves a better schedulability bound than
the Deferrable Server: PE avoids the back-to-back effect by degrading
unused capacity to lower priority levels over time, rather than
holding it at high priority until the period ends. Previously I had
conflated PE and DS as similar bandwidth-preserving mechanisms;
the trade-off between schedulability and aperiodic response time is
now clearer. Also useful was the historical context that PE is
mostly of theoretical importance today because Sporadic Server
achieves comparable bounds with simpler implementation. For deeper
study I will consult Buttazzo's textbook and the original 1989 paper
to verify the schedulability formula and explore numerical examples
before treating any of this material as canonical.
